head: 11f7ad94de7fe9a47a10a57f0bb3058b8ff88cdc
summary:
The core choice is sound and fits the record. The scanner thread publishes immutable snapshots, so nothing reads the live store, and that avoids both no-go spikes. The window meets all three conditions from the conditional spike. The two external behaviours the refresh rule depends on check out: DispatcherTimer defaults to Background priority (dotnet/wpf source), and Loaded priority runs after layout and render (Microsoft Learn's DispatcherPriority page). No blockers. The defects are in the invariants, and several hold only if every call site remembers them.

1. A folder's pending count is decremented at more than one place: a credit "on every exit" from a listing, plus Unreadable "wherever a folder is recorded as unreadable". A folder that fails to open can therefore be counted down twice. When that makes a row Done too early, no planned test notices.
2. The declared immutability rule misses public fields, `IList<>` properties, and a Rows list that shares its array with the tracker. Yet immutability is the whole thread-safety argument.
3. Two of the listed test cases have no way to be produced: an in-flight deeper listing interrupted on local NTFS, and a final snapshot arriving right after a skipped tick.

Smaller gaps:
- Finish relies on every return path remembering to call it.
- Cancelling during the root listing leaves an empty list even though files were read.
- There is no stated policy for what happens if the tracker throws.
- Snapshot state can leak from one scan to the next, and no one-scan-per-process window case can see it.
- The named fallback for a scan-time miss does not act on the per-listing cost.
- No test tree for the new rows includes a compressed/sparse file or a long path.
- Nobody owns the promised ListBox re-measure at 100k rows.
- The `.Store` rule has not been run against trunk.

findings.claim: The pending-folder count is decremented at more than one kind of call site, so a folder can be counted down twice. Listed(folder, pushed) adjusts pending by pushed-1 and is made 'on every exit from a listing, including an interrupted one'. Unreadable(folder) also decrements, 'wherever a folder is recorded as unreadable'. A folder whose open fails is both an exit from a listing and a folder recorded as unreadable, so a finally-block Listed plus an in-place Unreadable subtracts 2. The same risk applies to a folder cancelled mid-listing: the record has separate CancelledFolderTests, so the scanner records that case distinctly, and routing it through the unreadable path would also add a false 'could not be opened' to UnreadableBelow. A double decrement either leaves pending below zero, so the row is stuck at Reading (the completed-scan test catches that), or reaches 0 while subfolders are still queued, so the row shows Done while it keeps growing (nothing catches that; see M2). Whether this happens depends on the builder remembering it at every site that records an unreadable or cancelled folder, and at any separate long-path listing branch.
findings.evidence: Design, TopLevelTracker: 'adjust pending by (subfolders actually pushed for F) - 1. A folder that could not be opened decrements pending'. Scanner hook-up: 'The credit is made on every exit from a listing, including an interrupted one ... Calls tracker.Unreadable(folder) wherever a folder is recorded as unreadable.' Survey C3 lists CancelledFolderTests.
findings.fix: Replace Listed and Unreadable with one entry point, tracker.FolderExited(folder, outcome, subfoldersPushed), where outcome is Listed, Unreadable or Interrupted. Call it from a single finally around each folder's listing in Scanner.cs, so each folder is decremented exactly once by construction and a cancelled folder is never counted as unreadable. Add Debug.Assert(pending >= 0) in the tracker.

findings.claim: No planned test detects a row that goes Done too early. The completed-scan test checks only the end state. The monotonic-state test allows Done to Done. The row-sum test checks only that each snapshot adds up to its own sums. A row that reaches Done while its subtree is still being read, and keeps growing afterwards, passes all of them. Yet 'Done' is the one state that tells the person a figure is final.
findings.evidence: Core row tests: 'every snapshot's rows add up to its own sums and states only move NotRead to Reading to Done ... At Completed no Reading or NotRead folder row remains'.
findings.fix: Add one assertion to the AfterFolder snapshot loop that already exists: once a row is Done (or Unreadable or NotFollowed) in snapshot k, its Bytes, OnDisk, Files, Folders, UnreadableBelow and State are identical in every later snapshot. Run it on the unreadable-deeper-folder tree and the link-folder tree, the two shapes most likely to double-decrement.

findings.claim: The design calls immutability 'the whole thread-safety argument', but the rule declared to enforce it does not catch the ways immutability is likely to break. (a) Public mutable fields (`public long Bytes;`) match none of the three patterns. (b) `public IList<TopLevelRow>` or `ICollection<>` properties pass, because only List, Dictionary, HashSet and ObservableCollection are named. (c) The most likely defect is aliasing, and it lives in TopLevelTracker.cs, not TopLevelSnapshot.cs. The design has the tracker keep a published-row array and 'reuse unchanged row objects'. If the snapshot constructor stores the caller's array as its IReadOnlyList, the tracker's in-place replacement of dirty rows changes every snapshot it has already published. A consumer can also cast an array-backed IReadOnlyList back to T[] and sort it in place. The held-snapshot test catches (c) only on the paths it exercises. Later slices that add fields to TopLevelRow are guarded only by this regex.
findings.evidence: architecture_rules 'published snapshot types cannot be changed after they are built': must_not_match ['\bset\s*;', '\bpublic\s+(?:List|Dictionary|HashSet|ObservableCollection)<', '\bpublic\s+\w+\[\]\s+\w+'], files: src/FsAnalyser.Core/TopLevelSnapshot.cs only. Decision: 'Unchanged row objects are reused'; 'costs one array of references plus the few dirty rows per publish'.
findings.fix: Enforce it in the seam. The TopLevelSnapshot constructor copies its rows into a private array and exposes it as Array.AsReadOnly(copy), which cannot be cast back. That copy is the same one-array-per-publish cost the design already budgets. Extend the rule with a public-field pattern (e.g. '\bpublic\s+(?!const\b|static\b|readonly\b|override\b|abstract\b|sealed\b|class\b|record\b|enum\b|struct\b|interface\b)[\w.<>\[\],?]+\s+\w+\s*[;=]') and with '\bpublic\s+I(?:List|Collection|Dictionary|Set)<'.

findings.claim: Two listed case shapes have no way to be produced, and the design names none. (1) 'Cancel arrives while a folder listing is in flight and SynchronousIoCancel interrupts it', with partial adds already in the running totals, in a Core test on a real temp NTFS tree in the default filter. Listing a local NTFS directory does not block, so nothing is in flight long enough to cancel. The only stall mechanisms on record are the opt-in SMB loopback, StallRig, and whatever makes CancelReturnsFromAScanStuckInItsFirstCall stick in the root's first call. None of them is shown to produce a deeper listing that is interrupted after appending some entries. This is the case that guards the synthesis's own 'credit on every exit' amendment, so without it the amendment goes unverified. (2) 'the final snapshot arriving right after a skipped tick'. A skip needs a refresh over 100 ms, but sorting and re-binding thousands of rows takes milliseconds (spike 2: p95 17.6 ms at 100k). There is no App test project and no hook to force a skip, so the rule that the skip must never swallow the ending cannot be exercised.
findings.evidence: Cases: 'cancel a scan / Cancel arrives while a folder listing is in flight and SynchronousIoCancel interrupts it'; 'refresh the list under load / ... with the final snapshot arriving right after a skipped tick'. Core row tests 'Runs in the default filter'. Survey: N-001..N-004 and StalledShareTests are opt-in and were not run.
findings.fix: For (1), name the seam in the design: an internal ScanOptions callback invoked inside the enumeration loop after N entries of a chosen folder, which cancels the token and forces the interrupted exit path. If the stuck-first-call mechanism works on a deeper folder, say so explicitly. For (2), add a hook environment variable, e.g. FSA_HOOK_SLOW_REFRESH_MS, that pads ShowTopLevel so a skip occurs. Or drop the shape from the cases and record it as unverified.

findings.claim: 'Calls tracker.Finish(completed) on every path that returns a ScanResult' is a rule every return path must remember. If one path forgets (the root first-call cancel path, the fault-adjacent paths, or a return added later), ScanResult.TopLevel is null or not final. The ending handler then clears the list, and the person loses the rows they watched fill in, on exactly the Cancel path where the slice promises to keep what was read.
findings.evidence: Scanner hook-up: 'Calls tracker.Finish(completed) on every path that returns a ScanResult.' Contract ScanResult.TopLevel: 'Null only when the root itself was never listed.'
findings.fix: Make the ScanResult constructor take the final snapshot as a required argument, and call tracker.Finish inside the one method that builds ScanResult (Run.Finish). A missed call then cannot compile.

findings.claim: The tracker is created only after the root listing returns. A Cancel that interrupts the root listing itself (a huge flat root, or a slow share root) therefore leaves ScanResult.TopLevel null, even though the scanner appended and counted some root children. The window shows counters with files read and the header 'What was read before the stop' over an empty list. The contract says null means 'the root itself was never listed', which is not true here. Any Moved or Unreadable call made during the root listing (e.g. two root-level names of one hardlink with a stale size) would also hit a null tracker.
findings.evidence: Scanner hook-up: 'Creates the tracker after the root listing returns.' Contract: 'Null only when the root itself was never listed.' Case 'end a scan with nothing to show' covers only an already-cancelled token, an unopenable root and an empty root.
findings.fix: Create the tracker at scan start, and seed rows on every exit from the root listing, interrupted exits included (the same rule the design already applies to deeper listings). Rows from a partial root listing start NotRead. Add the interrupted-root shape to the cancel cases once M4's seam exists.

findings.claim: The design adds new code inside the counting-critical scanner loop (Parent walks, row lookup, Moved) but says nothing about what happens if that code throws, e.g. an index miss in the row lookup or a Parent walk that never reaches the root. The exception reaches Scanner.Scan and the whole scan faults, costing the counts the SL-020 code would have finished correctly. Whether the tracker should fail loudly or fail contained is a decision the design leaves to the builder.
findings.evidence: TopLevelTracker 'Called only from the Scanner run loop on the scanner's own thread'. There is no error_cases entry for tracker faults in any contract.
findings.fix: State the policy. Recommended: tracker faults are caught at the tracker boundary; the tracker disables itself and publishes nothing more; ScanResult.TopLevel is null, so the list clears; the scan continues; Debug.Fail makes tests fail loudly.

findings.claim: The view skips a refresh when 'Sequence is unchanged', and Sequence restarts with every scan. If the last-shown Sequence is not reset at scan start, the new scan's first snapshot with the same number is skipped. If ScanProgress is reused across scans, the previous scan's final snapshot sits in TopLevel until the new root listing returns, and the first tick shows the old drive's rows under the new root's 'so far' header. The design never states that ScanProgress is created per scan. Every window case launches one scan per process, so no case can catch this.
findings.evidence: Results list: 'on a timer tick it does nothing if Sequence is unchanged ... Scan start clears the list'. Contract TopLevelSnapshot: 'Sequence (rises with each publish)'.
findings.fix: Compare snapshots by reference (ReferenceEquals with the last shown one), not by Sequence. State in the contract that each scan gets a new ScanProgress. Have ShowTopLevel ignore a snapshot whose Root differs from the running scan's root.

findings.claim: The design says 'A measured miss means a coarser publish cadence inside the tracker, not a new boundary.' But publishing happens at most every 250 ms and costs one array copy. The work that scales with the scan is per listing: a Parent walk from F to the root through ScanStore accessors (which spike 1 says volatile-read _count on every call), plus the credit and the time check. A coarser publish cadence does not reduce that, so the named fallback does not act on the likely cause of a miss.
findings.evidence: key_decisions 'Verification ...': 'It is expected to be under 2%. A measured miss means a coarser publish cadence'. Tracker: 'For each deeper folder listing F: walk Parent from F up to the root'. Spike 1 detail: 'volatile-reading _count in every accessor'.
findings.fix: Name the fallback that works: carry the top-row index on the scanner's stack entry, set when root children are pushed and inherited by descendants. The lookup is then O(1) with no store reads. Or keep the Parent walk but record in the design note that the measured cost is per listing.

findings.claim: The project constraint says the counting rules are 'the one place not to cut corners', and this slice creates a new output that carries them: per-row Bytes and OnDisk. The case list marks on-disk size and long paths as not material. But the row-sum test proves rows equal Totals only for the trees it runs on. A tree with no compressed or sparse file makes the OnDisk sum trivially equal. A tree with no path over 260 characters never exercises a separate long-path listing branch, if the scanner has one, and that branch would need its own exit credit.
findings.evidence: Case 'carry counting-rule figures through to rows', material: false: 'The tracker adds deltas and never branches on how a size was computed'. Constraint (testing): 'Links not followed, hardlinks counted once, on-disk size, long paths and unreadable folders must each have a test on a real temporary folder tree'.
findings.fix: Put one NTFS-compressed file and one path over 260 characters under a top-level folder in the existing completed-scan row-sum tree. Assert that row OnDisk < row Bytes for that row, and that rows equal Totals. No new test class is needed.

findings.claim: The spike's pass was measured on a TreeView stand-in at 100k children. The design says 'the build re-measures it' for the ListBox, but no component, case or design-note field owns that measurement. The design note records only scan time, and the thousands-row window case checks realized containers, not tick or Input-probe time. The coherence_check lists the ListBox-at-100k behaviour as not verified, so the conditional's numbers end up applied to a control nobody measured.
findings.evidence: key_decisions: 'a ListBox is the lighter of the two ... and the build re-measures it'. Design note: 'Records the scan-time measurement taken at build'. Spike 2: tick p95 17.6 ms and Input p95 30 ms, measured on a TreeView.
findings.fix: Have the watch-mode hook log each ShowTopLevel duration and an Input-priority probe delay during a run over a root with 100k children. Record p95 against the spike's 100 ms and 200 ms limits in docs/design/SL-039-live-results.md.

findings.claim: The rule 'the window never touches the scan store' forbids '\.Store\b' across all App .cs files, including legitimate post-scan reads, which have no concurrent writer. Nobody has run it against trunk. The survey found no mid-scan store reader, but it did not report whether the ending code (unreadable list, report writer) reads result.Store after the scan. If it does, the rule fails on code this slice does not touch. The pattern also misses property-pattern access such as `result is { Store: var s }`.
findings.evidence: architecture_rules: files 'src/FsAnalyser.App/**/*.cs', must_not_match ['\bScanStore\b', '\.Store\b']. Survey: 'No live results view and no mid-scan store reader'.
findings.fix: Before declaring the rule, run its patterns over trunk's src/FsAnalyser.App: Select-String -Path src/FsAnalyser.App -Recurse -Pattern '\bScanStore\b|\.Store\b|\bStore\s*:'. Add '\bStore\s*:' to the rule.

dimensions_checked.result: m5: the named fallback for a scan-time miss does not act on the per-listing cost. The biggest assumption is the design's own decidable disagreement: whether the running totals carry CorrectSizes deltas and an interrupted listing's partial adds, and whether ScanResult.Totals is the final running total. It is correctly flagged and sent to build's first step. The build-check stage opened Scanner.cs and was the node that could have recorded those facts; it cited only :60, :139, :163 and :165. The sum invariant holds by construction if Totals equals the final running total (the survey measured progress-final equal to Totals, but only on a tree with no hardlinks). Only attribution through Moved depends on the unread code, so 'would_force_resynthesis' looks overstated. Single-thread and depth-first claims rest on the record (Scanner.cs:12, spike 3).

m2: an interrupted root listing gives a null TopLevel although Totals > 0, and a Moved or Unreadable call before the tracker exists would hit null. Checked and found handled: an empty root, an unopenable root, an already-cancelled token, link folders never pushed, a top folder that cannot be opened, and a deeper unreadable folder. 'At most one StoppedPartway' relies on depth-first order, which Scanner.cs:12 confirms.

M1: pending decremented at several call sites, so an unreadable or cancelled folder can be counted down twice. m1: Finish relies on every return path remembering to call it. Both should move into one seam.

none: the throttle and row reuse are justified by the root-with-100k-children case from spike 2 and U-001. The six row states each map to a promise of honest labelling. A second window case and a report extension follow the recorded testing constraint. No new project, library or tool.

m4: comparing Sequence across scans and possibly reusing ScanProgress can show the previous scan's rows, and no one-scan-per-process window case can catch it. Contracts for TopLevel null, Final and Completed are otherwise stated. The report stays counts-only and within Q-016.
m3: no policy for a tracker exception on the scanner thread, which would fault a scan the counting code could have finished. The fault ending (hook 'throw' mode) clearing the list is designed.

m7: the promised ListBox re-measure at 100k rows has no owner or artifact. The two no-go spikes are respected: nothing reads the live store, and neither needs-first item is claimed. The conditional spike's three conditions are applied. Q-010 is followed (rules are appended). Q-001 is followed (symlinks with the unprivileged flag, never skipped). I did not re-raise the open one-level-versus-drill-down question; it is on the list.

M3: the immutability rule has gaps (public fields, IList<>, a Rows list sharing the tracker's array). m6: no row-level test tree includes a compressed/sparse file or a long path, although this slice touches the scanner. m8: the '.Store' rule has not been run against trunk. The no-lock tracker rule and the Volatile publication inside the ScanProgress property both hold by construction.

M2: no test catches a row that goes Done too early (Done should never change afterwards). M4: the in-flight deeper-listing cancel on local NTFS and the final-snapshot-after-a-skipped-tick shape have no way to be produced. What would settle them: a Core test with an enumeration-loop cancel seam, and a window run with a forced slow refresh.

none: a local single-user app. The report gains aggregate counts only, with no names or paths, matching Q-016, and the window case asserts that. The watch hook loads only through DOTNET_STARTUP_HOOKS, the mechanism already recorded. No new network, privilege or file-write surface. Citation check: the design as shown (clipped at 30,000 chars) carries no cited or recalled prior-art entries, so I checked the external WPF behaviour the refresh rule depends on instead. DispatcherTimer's default priority is Background (github.com/dotnet/wpf/blob/main/src/Microsoft.DotNet.Wpf/src/WindowsBase/System/Windows/Threading/DispatcherTimer.cs: 'this(DispatcherPriority.Background)'). Loaded priority (6) runs after layout and render (learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.windows.threading.dispatcherpriority). Both support the Loaded-priority end marker and the skip measurement. A Stack Overflow report (stackoverflow.com/questions/4793030) suggests replacing ItemsSource does not reset the scroll offset, so restoring VerticalOffset is harmless.
